prompt: City councils should make all public transport free of charge so that fewer people drive into city centres. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
text:
Traffic congestion and air pollution are persistent problems in many cities, and it is tempting to believe that abolishing fares would solve them. While free public transport could persuade some motorists to leave their cars at home, I largely disagree that it should be made universally free, because the policy is costly and other measures would reduce city-center driving more effectively.

The main argument in favor of free fares is that cost is a significant factor in how people choose to travel. If a bus or train ticket costs nothing, commuters who currently drive may reconsider, particularly when they must also pay for fuel and parking. Tallinn, the capital of Estonia, introduced free travel for residents in 2013 and recorded a rise in ridership, which suggests that price can influence behavior. Free services would also benefit low-income residents, who would gain easier access to jobs and education.

Nevertheless, the policy has serious drawbacks. Fares are a major source of revenue, and without them councils would have to finance services through higher taxes or cuts elsewhere. Reduced funding often leads to overcrowded vehicles and infrequent services, which discourages the very drivers the scheme is meant to attract. Moreover, evidence indicates that many new passengers are former walkers and cyclists rather than drivers, so the environmental gain is smaller than expected. Motorists tend to value convenience and comfort more than price.

A more effective strategy would combine reasonably priced, reliable public transport with measures that make driving less attractive. Congestion charges, as in London, have reduced traffic in the center while generating money that can be invested in new routes and modern vehicles. Park-and-ride facilities and dedicated bus lanes would further shorten journey times, giving commuters a practical reason to switch. Targeted discounts for students, pensioners and the unemployed could address fairness without sacrificing income.

In conclusion, although free public transport might attract some drivers, its financial burden and limited impact make it an inefficient solution. Councils should instead invest in quality and discourage car use directly.

prompt: Some people believe that schools should teach practical skills such as cooking and managing money, while others think schools should concentrate on academic subjects. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
text:
People disagree about whether schools should prioritize hands-on life skills, such as preparing meals and handling personal finances, or devote their limited time mainly to traditional academic disciplines. While a strong grounding in subjects like mathematics, science, and literature remains essential, I believe schools should also teach practical competencies because these are indispensable for adult independence and are often neglected at home.

Those who favor an academically focused curriculum argue that schools exist primarily to develop intellectual ability and prepare students for higher education and skilled employment. Mastery of core subjects equips young people with analytical thinking, literacy, and numeracy, which are transferable to almost any career. Moreover, school timetables are already crowded, so adding domestic or financial instruction may reduce time available for content that is examined and formally recognized by universities. For example, a student hoping to study engineering needs advanced mathematics and physics; if those lessons were reduced, his or her future opportunities could be narrowed.

However, supporters of practical education point out that many school leavers enter adulthood without the basic knowledge required to live responsibly. Understanding budgeting, saving, debt, nutrition, and simple cooking can protect young people from serious long-term problems, including poor health and financial hardship. These skills are not inferior to academic knowledge; rather, they complement it by enabling students to apply reasoning in everyday situations. For instance, a teenager who has learned how interest rates work is far less likely to accumulate unmanageable credit-card debt, while someone who can cook several inexpensive meals is less dependent on unhealthy convenience food.

In my view, schools should maintain academic rigor while incorporating a modest but compulsory program of life-skills education. This is especially important because not all families can teach these matters effectively, and schools are the one institution that reaches nearly every child. A balanced curriculum would therefore produce graduates who are not only knowledgeable but also capable of managing real-world responsibilities. Ultimately, education should prepare students not just to pass examinations, but to lead competent, self-sufficient lives.

prompt: More and more employees now work from home for most of the week. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
text:
The steady rise in remote work has transformed the modern labor market. Although working from home carries genuine drawbacks, I believe that its benefits for both employees and employers ultimately outweigh them, provided that organizations manage the arrangement thoughtfully.

The most compelling advantage is the improvement in time use and personal wellbeing. Commuting can consume two or three hours of a worker's day, and eliminating this journey frees time for exercise, family, or rest. A widely cited study of a Chinese travel agency, for instance, found that employees who worked remotely were not only happier but also completed more calls than their office-based colleagues. Employers benefit as well, since reduced demand for office space lowers rent and utility costs, while a wider geographic pool of candidates makes recruitment easier.

A second advantage concerns the broader environment and society. Fewer commuters mean less traffic congestion and lower carbon emissions, which is particularly valuable in crowded cities. Moreover, people who are no longer tied to expensive urban centers can settle in smaller towns, which revitalizes local economies and eases pressure on housing markets.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages should not be dismissed. Isolation is a serious concern, because casual conversations in corridors often spark ideas and build trust that video calls rarely replicate. Junior staff may suffer most, since they learn by observing experienced colleagues. In addition, the boundary between work and home can blur, leaving some employees answering messages late at night and struggling to switch off, which may eventually lead to burnout.

However, these problems are largely solvable. Companies can require occasional days in the office for collaboration, establish clear expectations about working hours, and organize mentoring schemes for newcomers. Such measures preserve the social fabric of the workplace without sacrificing flexibility.

In conclusion, remote work offers substantial gains in productivity, cost savings, and quality of life, while its main weaknesses can be mitigated through sensible policies. On balance, the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

prompt: In many countries, large amounts of food are thrown away by shops and households every day. Why does this happen, and what can be done to reduce it?
text:
The daily disposal of edible food by retailers and families has become a serious problem in many societies. In my view, this waste stems mainly from commercial practices that encourage overbuying and from consumer attitudes that undervalue food; therefore, the most effective remedies are stronger redistribution systems, clearer labeling, and better habits at home.

One major cause lies in the way food is marketed and sold. Supermarkets routinely offer multipack discounts and maintain shelves that look perpetually abundant, because full displays are associated with quality and choice. As a result, stores often overstock perishable goods and remove items before they are actually unsafe to eat. At the same time, shoppers are tempted to purchase more than they need, particularly when oversized portions appear economical. For example, a family may buy a large bag of salad or a "buy one, get one free" package of yogurt, only to discard part of it a few days later.

A second reason is widespread confusion and carelessness in households. Many people misunderstand date labels, treating "best before" as though it meant "dangerous after," even though the phrase usually refers only to peak quality. Busy lifestyles also contribute: meals are changed at short notice, leftovers are forgotten in refrigerators, and few people plan purchases carefully. This pattern is especially common in urban areas, where relatively high incomes can weaken the incentive to use food efficiently. When throwing away a loaf of bread or a container of fruit seems trivial, waste quickly becomes routine.

To address this issue, governments and businesses should make it easier to redirect surplus food, while consumers should manage it more responsibly. Stores can donate unsold products to charities, sell imperfect produce at reduced prices, and use technology to predict demand more accurately. Public authorities can standardize date labeling and run campaigns on meal planning, portion control, and safe storage. In households, simple measures such as shopping with a list, freezing excess food, and turning leftovers into new dishes would make a substantial difference. If these practical steps are adopted, food waste could be reduced dramatically.

prompt: Children today spend several hours a day looking at screens. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or a negative development?
text:
It is now commonplace to see young people absorbed in tablets, smartphones, and televisions for much of the day. This trend stems chiefly from the ubiquity of affordable devices and the pressures of modern family life, and I believe that, on balance, it is a negative development, although it is not without some benefits.

The first reason for heavy screen use is sheer availability. Devices that were once luxuries are now found in nearly every household, and schools increasingly assign homework that must be completed online. A child who researches a project on a laptop may then drift into videos or games without noticing the passage of time. Moreover, the platforms themselves are designed to hold attention, using autoplay and endless feeds that make it difficult for young users to stop.

A second explanation lies in the circumstances of contemporary parenting. In many families both parents work long hours, and screens offer a convenient and inexpensive way of keeping children occupied. Safety concerns also play a part, since parents who fear for their children's safety outdoors often prefer them to stay indoors. For example, a parent in a crowded city apartment may hand over a tablet simply because there is no safe place nearby to play.

Despite some advantages, I regard the overall effect as harmful. Educational applications can certainly teach reading and mathematics, and online communication helps children maintain friendships. However, prolonged screen time displaces physical activity, which contributes to obesity and poor posture. It also disrupts sleep, because the blue light emitted by devices interferes with the production of melatonin, leaving children tired and unable to concentrate at school. Furthermore, time spent watching passively reduces opportunities for face-to-face interaction, which is essential for developing empathy and social skills.

In conclusion, children's extensive use of screens results from the widespread availability of technology and the practical demands placed on families. Although digital tools offer genuine educational value, the damage to health, sleep, and social development outweighs these gains unless adults set firm and consistent limits.

prompt: Governments should place a high tax on sugary drinks and unhealthy snacks in order to improve public health. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
text:
Taxing sugar-laden beverages and nutritionally poor snacks is often proposed as a way to improve public health. I largely agree with this approach because higher prices can reduce excessive consumption and encourage manufacturers to reformulate their products. However, such taxes are most effective when they form part of a broader health strategy rather than being treated as a complete solution.

The strongest argument in favor of these levies is that price influences behavior, especially in relation to nonessential items. When products that are high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats become more expensive, many consumers buy them less frequently or choose smaller quantities. This is particularly true among young people, who are highly responsive to price changes. Mexico, for instance, introduced a tax on sweetened drinks and subsequently recorded a decline in purchases, especially among lower-income households. Given the clear link between regular consumption of these products and obesity, diabetes, and heart disease, a well-designed tax can therefore produce meaningful health benefits.

A further advantage is that fiscal pressure can change the food industry itself. In order to avoid higher taxes or preserve market share, companies may reduce sugar content, shrink portion sizes, or invest in healthier alternatives. The United Kingdom’s soft-drink levy provides a useful example: many brands reformulated beverages before the measure even took full effect. As a result, public health can improve not only because people consume less junk food, but also because the products available become less harmful.

That said, critics are right to point out that such taxes can be regressive, since poorer families spend a larger share of their income on food. For this reason, governments should spend the revenue on subsidizing fruit and vegetables, funding school meals, and supporting nutrition education. If taxation is paired with these measures, it becomes far fairer and far more powerful.

Overall, I agree that governments should impose substantial taxes on sugary drinks and unhealthy snacks. Although this policy has limitations, it can discourage harmful consumption and drive positive industrial change, particularly when combined with wider public-health interventions.

prompt: Some people think that older people should be cared for by their own families, while others believe that the state should provide this care. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
text:
The question of who should look after the elderly has become increasingly pressing as populations age. While family care offers undeniable emotional benefits, I believe that the state must bear primary responsibility, with families playing a complementary role.

Those who favor family care emphasize the emotional bond between relatives. An elderly person living with a son or daughter is surrounded by familiar faces and shared memories, which can reduce the loneliness and depression that often afflict residents of institutions. Moreover, caring for parents is widely regarded as a moral duty, since parents once devoted years to raising their children. In many Asian societies, such as South Korea and India, multigenerational households remain common, and grandparents often help with child rearing, which strengthens family ties across generations.

Nevertheless, there are compelling reasons why the state should take the lead. Modern families are frequently unable to provide round-the-clock attention, because both spouses usually work and relatives may live in distant cities or even abroad. Furthermore, caring for a person with dementia or severe mobility problems requires professional training and specialized equipment. Without support, relatives can suffer exhaustion, financial strain, and damaged careers. Japan's long-term care insurance system illustrates a better approach: it funds trained nurses, day centers, and home visits, so that older citizens receive consistent, high-quality assistance regardless of their children's circumstances.

In my view, the most effective arrangement combines both sources of care, with the government providing the infrastructure and funding and families offering companionship and emotional support. Taxpayers contribute throughout their working lives, so it is reasonable that they should expect dignified care in return. At the same time, public services should be designed to enable, rather than replace, family involvement, for example by paying allowances to relatives who care for elderly members part-time or by offering respite services.

In conclusion, although families can give older people a warmth that no institution can match, they cannot be expected to shoulder the entire burden. The state should therefore guarantee professional care, while relatives remain an essential source of love and companionship.

prompt: Many small towns now depend on tourism as their main source of income. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
text:
In many small towns, tourism has become the principal engine of the local economy. Although this dependence can expose communities to seasonal instability and commercial pressures, I believe the benefits generally outweigh the drawbacks, provided that tourism is managed responsibly. In particular, it can generate employment where few alternatives exist and can also finance the preservation of places that might otherwise decline.

The strongest argument in favor of tourism is its capacity to create jobs and stimulate a wide range of related businesses. Visitors spend money not only on hotels and restaurants, but also on transport, retail, guided tours, and cultural events, allowing even a modest town to support numerous small enterprises. This is especially significant in places where agriculture or traditional industry has weakened. For example, a coastal town that once relied on fishing may now sustain guesthouses, cafes, and boat excursions, giving younger residents a reason to remain rather than move to larger cities in search of work.

A further advantage is that tourist revenue can help maintain local heritage and improve public infrastructure. Historic buildings, museums, parks, and festivals often survive because they attract paying visitors, and the taxes generated by these activities can be reinvested in roads, sanitation, and public spaces. As a result, residents benefit alongside tourists. A mountain village, for instance, may restore its old center and upgrade public transportation in order to welcome visitors, yet these improvements also enhance daily life for the local population.

Admittedly, reliance on tourism has clear disadvantages. Demand may collapse during economic downturns or health emergencies, and excessive development can erode the character that first attracted visitors. In some towns, rising rents and overcrowding can also make life more difficult for local people. Nevertheless, these problems stem less from tourism itself than from poor planning and overdependence on a single market segment. With sensible regulation, investment in year-round attractions, and limits on uncontrolled construction, many of these risks can be reduced.

Overall, while dependence on tourism brings vulnerabilities, its economic and social contributions are usually greater. For small towns with limited alternatives, it often represents not merely a source of income, but a practical route to renewal and long-term survival.

prompt: In many large cities, young people can no longer afford to buy or rent a home. What are the causes of this problem, and what solutions can you suggest?
text:
Housing costs in many metropolitan areas have risen so sharply that people in their twenties and thirties are increasingly priced out of both ownership and the rental market. This problem stems mainly from a persistent shortage of supply, combined with stagnant wages and speculative investment, and it can be addressed through large-scale construction, stronger regulation, and more targeted financial support.

The first cause is that new housing has failed to keep pace with population growth. Cities attract workers because they offer better jobs and services, yet restrictive zoning laws, lengthy approval procedures, and the high price of urban land make construction slow and expensive. When demand consistently outstrips supply, prices and rents inevitably climb. In London, for example, the number of new homes built each year has fallen well short of household formation for decades, and the resulting competition has pushed rents far beyond what most young tenants can bear.

A second cause lies in the gap between incomes and housing costs. Entry-level salaries have grown slowly, and many young people are employed on temporary or part-time contracts, which makes it difficult to save for a deposit or to qualify for a mortgage. Meanwhile, wealthy investors and overseas buyers often purchase properties as financial assets rather than as homes, which inflates prices further. Consequently, a young graduate may spend more than half of a monthly paycheck on rent and be unable to accumulate any savings at all.

Several measures could ease this situation. Governments should relax planning restrictions and encourage higher-density development near public transport, while also funding affordable housing directly, as Vienna has done successfully through its extensive municipal housing program. In addition, rent stabilization and higher taxes on vacant or speculative properties would discourage investors from treating housing purely as a commodity. Finally, deposit assistance schemes and shared-ownership models could help first-time buyers enter the market.

In conclusion, the housing crisis facing young urban residents is driven chiefly by inadequate supply, weak income growth, and speculation. Only a combination of expanded construction, tighter market regulation, and well-designed financial support is likely to restore affordability.

prompt: Fewer people read printed newspapers than in the past. Why is this happening? What effects does this have on society?
text:
The steady decline in printed newspaper readership is primarily the result of technological change and shifting consumer habits, and this trend has both beneficial and harmful consequences for society. Although the move away from paper has made news more accessible and immediate, it has also weakened the economic and civic foundations that traditional newspapers once supported.

The main reason fewer people buy printed papers is that digital media provide a faster, cheaper, and more convenient alternative. News websites, mobile applications, and social media platforms deliver updates around the clock, whereas a printed edition can become outdated within hours. In addition, many younger adults have grown up reading on screens and see little reason to pay for a physical product that must be purchased or delivered. For example, a commuter can now scan breaking stories, watch video reports, and receive personalized alerts on a phone during a train ride, something a printed paper cannot match.

One significant effect of this shift is greater public access to information. Because online content is often free or low-cost, people from a wider range of income groups can follow current events. Digital platforms also allow readers to compare sources instantly and to engage with global issues that may never have appeared in a local paper. During natural disasters, for instance, live online coverage and emergency notifications can spread crucial information far more quickly than the next morning's printed edition.

However, the decline of print journalism also carries serious social costs. Traditional newspapers historically funded investigative reporting through subscriptions and advertising, but that business model has been badly damaged by the migration of readers and advertisers online. As a result, many local newsrooms have shrunk or closed, leaving communities with less scrutiny of public officials and fewer reliable reports on schools, courts, and city government. In my view, this is the most troubling consequence, because a society without strong professional journalism becomes more vulnerable to misinformation and weaker democratic accountability.

In conclusion, printed newspapers are losing readers because digital media better suit modern life. While this change has expanded the speed and reach of news, it has also undermined the institutions that produce rigorous reporting, with profound implications for public trust and civic life.

prompt: Professional athletes are paid far too much money compared with people in other important jobs. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
text:
The salaries of elite athletes often dwarf those of nurses, teachers, and firefighters, and many people find this disparity offensive. While I understand the moral intuition behind this complaint, I only partially agree with it. The extraordinary earnings of top sports stars are explained largely by market forces, yet the gap in pay does reveal a genuine failure to reward socially vital work adequately.

On one hand, athletes' incomes reflect the revenue they generate rather than a judgment of their social worth. Sport is a global entertainment industry in which broadcasting rights, sponsorships, and merchandise sales generate billions of dollars. A player such as Lionel Messi attracts millions of viewers, and clubs that employ him recoup his salary through jersey sales and advertising. Moreover, athletic careers are short and precarious: most players retire in their mid-thirties, and a single injury can end their earning potential overnight. Their high pay therefore compensates for a very brief window of opportunity.

On the other hand, it is difficult to justify a system in which a midlevel footballer earns more in a week than a nurse earns in a year. Nurses, teachers, and paramedics contribute directly to public health, education, and safety, and societies depend on them far more than on any sporting event. Because such professionals are usually paid from public budgets rather than by consumers in a competitive market, their wages are determined by political priorities, which frequently favor short-term savings. In the United Kingdom, for instance, hospital staff have repeatedly gone on strike over pay while top-flight clubs have spent record sums on transfers.

The solution, however, lies not in capping athletes' earnings, which would be difficult to enforce and would simply drive talent to wealthier leagues abroad. Instead, governments should raise the pay of essential workers and could tax extreme incomes more progressively, directing the proceeds toward public services.

In conclusion, athletes are not overpaid in terms of the value the market assigns to them, but the disparity highlights how undervalued essential professions are. Correcting that imbalance should be the priority.

prompt: Some people say that money spent on space exploration would be better used to solve problems on Earth. Others believe that space research brings benefits to everyone. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
text:
It is often argued that the vast sums allocated to missions beyond our planet should instead be directed toward urgent terrestrial needs, while others contend that investigating space generates advantages for all humanity. Although both perspectives have merit, I believe that space research deserves continued funding because its long-term scientific and practical gains are substantial, provided that governments also meet their social responsibilities at home.

Those who oppose heavy expenditure on space programs usually point to the severity of problems already affecting human life. In many countries, poverty, inadequate health care, failing infrastructure, and environmental degradation demand immediate action, yet public budgets are finite. From this standpoint, financing rockets and planetary probes can appear morally questionable when citizens lack clean water or access to basic medical treatment. For example, a developing nation facing recurring floods might achieve far greater social benefit by investing in drainage systems, emergency shelters, and disease prevention than by contributing to an expensive satellite launch.

However, supporters of space exploration rightly emphasize that such research often produces innovations whose value extends far beyond astronomy. Technologies first developed for use in spacecraft have led to advances in communications, weather forecasting, navigation, materials science, and medical equipment. Satellites, in particular, now underpin everyday activities, from disaster monitoring to precision agriculture, enabling societies to use resources more efficiently and to protect lives. A clear example is the use of satellite imagery to predict hurricanes and track wildfires, which allows authorities to evacuate communities earlier and reduce casualties.

In my view, treating space research and earthly welfare as mutually exclusive is a false choice. Sensible governments should certainly avoid prestige projects that consume public money without clear purpose, especially where basic needs remain unmet. Nevertheless, abandoning space exploration would be short-sighted, since many of the tools needed to address climate change, food insecurity, and natural disasters are themselves products of that research. The most reasonable approach, therefore, is not to stop exploring space, but to fund it responsibly alongside sustained investment in solving pressing problems on Earth.

prompt: Some universities now offer entire degree courses online. Do the advantages of studying in this way outweigh the disadvantages?
text:
The rise of fully online degrees has transformed access to higher education. Although virtual study has real drawbacks, I believe that its advantages, particularly flexibility and affordability, generally outweigh them, provided that students are self-disciplined and institutions support them properly.

The most compelling advantage is flexibility. Online programs allow students to watch lectures and complete assignments at times that suit their schedules, which makes university education realistic for people who work full-time, raise children, or live far from a campus. For example, a nurse in a rural area can pursue a master's degree in public health without relocating or giving up her income. Such opportunities widen participation in higher education and make lifelong learning a practical option rather than an ideal.

Cost is a second significant benefit. Studying remotely eliminates expenses such as housing, commuting, and relocation, and many universities charge lower tuition for online courses because they need fewer physical facilities. Consequently, students graduate with less debt and can begin their careers sooner. Open University programs in Britain, which have enabled thousands of adults to earn degrees at modest cost, illustrate how effective this model can be.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages should not be dismissed. Learning online can be isolating, and the spontaneous discussions, friendships, and professional networks that develop on a campus are difficult to replicate through video calls. In addition, students who lack motivation may fall behind without the structure of fixed timetables, which partly explains why dropout rates in online courses are often higher than in traditional ones. Subjects that require laboratories or practical training, such as engineering or medicine, are also poorly suited to remote delivery.

However, these problems can be mitigated. Universities can organize virtual study groups, assign personal tutors, and combine online teaching with short residential sessions for practical work. Students, for their part, can develop time-management habits that will serve them well in any profession.

In conclusion, although online degrees cannot fully reproduce the social and practical richness of campus life, their flexibility and lower cost make higher education accessible to far more people. For this reason, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

prompt: Many people today feel stressed by their jobs. What are the main reasons for this, and how can employers and individuals deal with it?
text:
Work-related stress has become a defining feature of modern employment, affecting people in occupations ranging from finance to health care. In my view, this pressure stems chiefly from excessive demands and from the erosion of boundaries between professional and private life. Although the problem is serious, it can be mitigated if organizations redesign jobs more responsibly and if workers adopt deliberate habits to protect their well-being.

One major cause is that many employees are expected to produce more with fewer resources. Companies often operate with lean staffing, aggressive targets, and constant performance monitoring, all of which create a sense of permanent urgency. When workers feel that any mistake may damage their appraisal or even their job security, ordinary responsibilities become psychologically exhausting. This is particularly evident in hospitals, where nurses frequently manage too many patients during a shift; under such conditions, even highly skilled professionals can experience chronic anxiety and burnout.

A second source of strain is the growing difficulty of disconnecting from work. Digital technology has made it possible, and in some workplaces implicitly necessary, to answer messages at night, attend virtual meetings across time zones, and remain available during vacations. As a result, recovery time is interrupted and personal relationships suffer. For example, a marketing executive who is expected to reply to clients throughout the evening may never fully relax, despite technically having left the office hours earlier.

Employers can address this by setting realistic workloads, increasing managerial support, and establishing clear policies on after-hours communication. Providing counseling services and training supervisors to recognize early signs of distress would also help. Individuals, meanwhile, should strengthen their own coping strategies by setting boundaries, prioritizing tasks, exercising regularly, and seeking assistance before pressure becomes overwhelming. If a software engineer, for instance, turns off notifications after a fixed hour and discusses deadlines early, both productivity and mental health are likely to improve.

Overall, job stress is driven primarily by excessive workload and constant connectivity. However, with structural reforms from employers and disciplined self-management from employees, it is entirely possible to create healthier and more sustainable working lives.

prompt: In some countries, people are getting married and having children later in life than before. What are the reasons for this? Is it a positive or negative development?
text:
In many societies, men and women now marry and start families well into their thirties, whereas previous generations typically did so in their early twenties. This shift stems mainly from lengthier education, economic pressures, and changing social values. Although it brings certain benefits, I believe that on balance it is a positive development, provided that governments offer adequate support.

The first group of causes is economic and educational. Young people now spend longer in universities, and many pursue postgraduate degrees before they begin their careers. Once employed, they face expensive housing and unstable contracts, which makes starting a household seem risky. In cities such as London or Seoul, for instance, the average deposit for a home exceeds several years of a young person's salary, so couples often postpone marriage until they feel financially secure.

Cultural change is equally important. Marriage is no longer regarded as a social obligation or the only route to adulthood, and women in particular have gained access to professional opportunities that were once closed to them. Many therefore prioritize career advancement and personal independence before committing to a partner. Effective contraception has also given people greater control over when to have children.

In my view, the advantages of this trend outweigh its drawbacks. Couples who marry later tend to be more emotionally mature and financially stable, which can create a calmer environment for raising children. Research in several countries has linked later marriage with lower divorce rates, and parents with established careers are better able to provide for their children's education. Moreover, delaying parenthood allows women to build careers without interruption.

Nevertheless, there are genuine concerns. Fertility declines with age, so some couples struggle to conceive, and persistently low birth rates can lead to ageing populations and a shrinking workforce. Older parents may also have less energy to raise young children. These problems, however, can be mitigated through affordable fertility treatment, generous parental leave, and subsidized childcare.

In conclusion, later marriage and parenthood result chiefly from extended education, economic insecurity, and evolving attitudes. Despite some demographic risks, the trend is largely beneficial, because it enables individuals to make more considered and better-prepared life choices.

prompt: City councils should make all public transport free of charge so that fewer people drive into city centres. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
text:
I largely agree that municipal authorities should remove fares from buses, trams, and urban rail in order to reduce car use in downtown areas. Although free travel alone will not persuade every driver to leave a private vehicle at home, it would significantly lower one of the main barriers to using public transit and would bring wider social benefits that justify the policy.

The strongest argument in favor of free transit is that price matters, especially for commuters who make frequent journeys. Even modest daily fares accumulate into a substantial monthly expense, so many people who already own a car may conclude that driving is more convenient and only slightly more costly. If transit were free, however, the financial comparison would change immediately, making buses and trains the more attractive option for students, office workers, and low-income residents. In Tallinn, for example, the introduction of fare-free public transportation for residents was followed by higher ridership, showing that cost can influence travel behavior.

A second reason to support the proposal is that fewer cars in central districts would produce benefits far beyond traffic reduction. Lower vehicle volumes mean cleaner air, less noise, and streets that are safer for pedestrians and cyclists. City centers could then become more appealing places to work, shop, and live. This is particularly important in densely populated areas where congestion imposes heavy economic and environmental costs. If fewer commuters drove into the core of a city such as London or Seoul, businesses would also gain from more reliable journey times for deliveries and essential services.

That said, free transport is not a complete solution. Some motorists will continue to drive because they value privacy, flexibility, or speed, especially if services are overcrowded or unreliable. For this reason, fare abolition should be accompanied by investment in frequency, cleanliness, and network coverage, as well as measures such as parking restrictions and congestion charges.

Overall, I agree to a great extent that city councils should make public transportation free. While the policy must be part of a broader urban strategy, it is a practical and socially beneficial way to discourage car use in city centers.

prompt: Some people believe that schools should teach practical skills such as cooking and managing money, while others think schools should concentrate on academic subjects. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
text:
Education systems around the world face a perennial question about what young people ought to learn. Some argue that classrooms should prepare students for daily life by teaching skills such as cooking and budgeting, whereas others maintain that schools should devote their time to traditional academic disciplines. While both positions have merit, I believe the most effective approach is to keep academic study at the core of the curriculum and to add a modest, well-structured program of practical instruction.

Advocates of academic subjects make a persuasive case. Mathematics, science, literature and history develop analytical reasoning, disciplined writing and the capacity for abstract thought, abilities that underpin university study and most professional careers. Because instructional hours are limited, adding new subjects inevitably reduces time for these foundations. Finland, for example, is often admired for its rigorous core teaching, which equips graduates to adapt to rapidly changing industries. Moreover, teachers are trained as subject specialists, and many families lack the resources to provide enriching academic experiences at home, so schools remain the only dependable place to acquire them.

Nevertheless, supporters of practical education highlight a genuine gap. Many young adults leave school with excellent examination results yet cannot prepare a nutritious meal, compare loan interest rates or draw up a monthly budget. The consequences are considerable: poor diets contribute to health problems, and financial illiteracy leads to unmanageable debt. Parents are not always able to fill this void, since some may lack these skills themselves. In the United Kingdom, the introduction of compulsory financial education in secondary schools was a direct response to such concerns, and early evidence suggests that students feel more confident handling money.

In my view, these two aims are not mutually exclusive. Practical lessons need only occupy a small portion of the timetable, and they can even reinforce academic learning. Cooking, for instance, applies chemistry and fractions, while budgeting gives arithmetic a tangible purpose. Integrating such activities into existing subjects or offering a short weekly course would therefore enrich education without sacrificing intellectual rigor.

In conclusion, although academic subjects must remain the priority because they build lasting cognitive abilities, schools also have a responsibility to prepare students for independent adulthood. A balanced curriculum that combines both elements serves individuals and society best.

prompt: More and more employees now work from home for most of the week. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
text:
The growing prevalence of working from home for much of the week has transformed the modern labor market. While this arrangement can create difficulties related to coordination and employee well-being, I believe its benefits are more significant overall because it offers substantial gains in productivity, flexibility, and access to employment.

One major advantage is that remote work often allows people to use their time far more efficiently. Without a daily commute, employees can devote those saved hours to work, family responsibilities, or rest, all of which may improve concentration and output. In addition, many people perform better in a quiet, personalized environment than in a crowded office filled with interruptions. For example, a software developer who works from home may complete complex tasks more quickly because uninterrupted periods of deep focus are easier to achieve than in an open-plan workplace.

A second benefit is that home-based employment greatly expands opportunity for both workers and employers. Companies are no longer restricted to hiring people who live near their offices, and employees can apply for positions in other cities without relocating. This is particularly valuable for parents of young children, people with disabilities, and those living in rural areas, all of whom may find daily travel difficult. A marketing firm in New York, for instance, can employ a highly skilled designer in a small town in Colorado, thereby gaining talent that would otherwise be unavailable.

Admittedly, there are disadvantages. Some remote workers feel isolated, and collaboration can become less spontaneous when all communication is scheduled through video calls or messaging platforms. However, these problems can be reduced through regular in-person meetings, well-structured online teamwork, and managerial support for mental health. Since such measures are increasingly common, the drawbacks are manageable rather than fundamental.

In conclusion, although working from home presents challenges, the advantages outweigh them. The model saves time, raises efficiency, and makes employment more inclusive, so it is ultimately a positive development for most employees and organizations.

prompt: In many countries, large amounts of food are thrown away by shops and households every day. Why does this happen, and what can be done to reduce it?
text:
Every day, enormous quantities of perfectly edible food end up in the trash, both in stores and in private kitchens. This problem stems mainly from commercial practices and from careless consumer habits, but it can be reduced through stricter regulation and a change in public attitudes.

One major cause lies in the way retailers operate. Supermarkets strive to keep their shelves full at all times, because customers tend to avoid stores that look empty. As a result, they order more than they can realistically sell, and surplus items are discarded once they approach their expiration dates. Furthermore, produce that is misshapen or slightly blemished is frequently rejected, since shoppers are believed to prefer flawless fruit and vegetables. In some countries, entire harvests of crooked carrots or small apples never reach the market for this reason.

Households contribute to the problem in different ways. Many people buy in bulk to take advantage of special offers, yet they lack the time to plan meals or to use everything before it spoils. Confusion over date labels worsens matters, as the phrase "best before" is often mistaken for a safety deadline, so wholesome products are thrown away unnecessarily. A family that purchases a large quantity of bread and milk, for instance, may discard half of it within a week.

Several measures could help. Governments can follow the example of France, where large supermarkets are legally prohibited from destroying unsold food and must donate it to charities instead. Clearer labeling and public campaigns could also teach consumers to distinguish between quality and safety dates. At home, individuals can write shopping lists, store leftovers properly and compost any scraps that remain, which would reduce both their expenses and their environmental impact.

In conclusion, food waste results from the pursuit of perfect appearance and constant availability in shops, together with poor planning in homes. Legislation, education and more thoughtful personal habits, working together, can substantially reduce the amount of food that is wasted.

prompt: Children today spend several hours a day looking at screens. Why is this the case? Is this a positive or a negative development?
text:
In many countries, young people now devote a substantial part of each day to phones, tablets, computers, and televisions. This trend has emerged because digital devices are woven into both education and leisure, and because they offer parents a convenient form of supervision in increasingly busy households. Although screens can support learning and communication, I believe their growing dominance in children’s lives is, on balance, a negative development.

One major reason for the rise in screen use is that technology has become indispensable at school and at home. Homework is often assigned and submitted online, lessons rely on educational platforms, and even reading materials are frequently digital rather than printed. At the same time, entertainment has shifted toward streaming services, video games, and short-form content designed to hold attention for long periods. For example, a child may spend the afternoon using a laptop for research, then switch to a gaming console or smartphone in the evening, meaning that screens occupy hours without any single session seeming excessive.

A second cause is the pressure on modern families. Many parents work long hours and have limited access to safe outdoor spaces or affordable extracurricular activities. In that context, a screen is an easy way to keep children occupied, quiet, and physically indoors. This is particularly true in large cities, where concerns about traffic or crime discourage unsupervised play. A tablet, therefore, often becomes a practical substitute for parks, sports, or face-to-face socializing.

Despite certain advantages, the overall impact is harmful. Excessive screen exposure can reduce physical activity, disrupt sleep, and weaken attention spans, especially when children constantly switch between apps and notifications. It may also displace experiences that are essential for healthy development, such as imaginative play, conversation, and direct contact with peers. While educational programs and video calls with relatives are undeniably valuable, these benefits do not outweigh the costs when digital media becomes the default way to spend free time.

In conclusion, children spend so much time in front of screens because technology now structures schooling, recreation, and family routines. Nevertheless, since this habit often replaces exercise, rest, and real-world interaction, it should be regarded as a negative trend overall.

prompt: Some universities now offer entire degree courses online. Do the advantages of studying in this way outweigh the disadvantages?
text:
The increasing availability of fully online degree programmes has transformed higher education, allowing students to obtain university qualifications without attending a physical campus. Although this approach presents certain challenges, particularly in terms of social interaction and practical training, I believe its advantages outweigh its disadvantages because it makes higher education more accessible, flexible and affordable.

One of the most significant benefits of online learning is that it removes geographical and financial barriers to education. Students living in remote areas or countries with limited educational opportunities can enrol at universities that would otherwise be inaccessible to them. Furthermore, studying remotely eliminates many of the expenses associated with attending university, such as accommodation and commuting costs. This is particularly beneficial for students from disadvantaged backgrounds, for whom relocating to another city or country may be financially unrealistic. Online programmes also enable working professionals and parents to pursue academic qualifications without giving up their employment or neglecting family responsibilities. Consequently, higher education becomes an opportunity available to a much broader section of society.

Admittedly, studying entirely online has its limitations. The absence of face-to-face interaction can leave students feeling isolated and may restrict their opportunities to develop interpersonal skills and professional networks. Moreover, certain disciplines, such as medicine and engineering, require practical experience that cannot be fully replicated through digital platforms. Nevertheless, these shortcomings vary considerably depending on the subject being studied. While online delivery may be unsuitable for courses involving extensive laboratory or clinical work, disciplines such as computer science, business and mathematics can often be taught effectively through interactive lectures, collaborative projects and virtual discussions. Universities can also provide academic support and opportunities for peer interaction through well-designed online learning environments.

In conclusion, despite the limitations of remote education, particularly in subjects requiring hands-on experience, its capacity to expand educational opportunities and accommodate students' individual circumstances is more significant. Provided that universities maintain rigorous academic standards and offer adequate support, online degree programmes represent a valuable and inclusive alternative to conventional higher education.

prompt: Advertisements aimed at children are common on television and the internet. Why do companies target children? Should this kind of advertising be banned?
text:
Advertising aimed at children has become increasingly common, especially on television and online platforms. Companies target young audiences for several commercial reasons. Although advertising can sometimes provide useful information, I believe that certain types of advertisements directed at children should be banned, while others should be strictly controlled.

The main reason why companies advertise to children is that they can easily influence their parents' spending decisions. When children see an attractive advertisement for a toy or a particular snack, they often ask their parents to buy it. Parents may eventually agree, even if they did not originally plan to purchase the product. Another important reason is that companies want to build brand loyalty from an early age. Children who become familiar with a particular brand may continue buying its products when they grow up. As a result, businesses can benefit from these customers for many years.

In my opinion, advertising aimed at children should be restricted because young people do not always have the ability to recognise commercial intentions. They may believe that owning certain products will make them happier or more popular among their friends. Moreover, advertisements for unhealthy food can encourage poor eating habits, which may lead to health problems in the future. Therefore, companies should not be allowed to promote such products directly to children.

However, a complete ban on children's advertising may not be necessary. Some advertisements promote educational products, books or activities that can be beneficial for children's development. Instead of banning all advertisements, governments should introduce clear regulations regarding their content and the way they are presented to young audiences.

In conclusion, companies target children because of their influence on family purchases and their potential value as future customers. While harmful advertising should be banned, responsible advertising could remain available under appropriate government supervision.
